First, we substitute $u={x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{2}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-{e}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{e}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/4844d6220d04a6a1fffdd5a485a9e6724aa6065397b8c3a009157a7a2dafc3cf.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
